message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) are both placental mammals, but they belong to different orders—Carnivora for lions and Perissodactyla for zebras. Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes many of the “big” land mammals that evolved on the northern supercontinent Laurasia.

In terms of time, this ancestor lived roughly **60–70 million years ago** during the Paleocene–Eocene transition. It would have been a small, insectivorous or omnivorous mammal, probably similar in size and ecology to modern-day shrews or small rodents. From this ancestor, the lineages that would become the diverse carnivores (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and the odd-toed ungulates (horses, rhinos, tapirs, etc.) split off and eventually gave rise to the modern lion and zebra, respectively.
